elements.char: We also investigated the samples in the tails of the histogram as they often came from
elements.label: text

elements.char: the edges of the training distribution.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Later work will investigate techniques to score the
elements.label: text

elements.char: likelihood that a sample of test data will produce an accurate valuation with kernel density
elements.label: text

elements.char: estimation and statistical measures of distance showing promise.

elements.char: Speed
elements.label: text

elements.char: The overall performance can be broken down into the three key phases, generation of the
elements.label: text

elements.char: training set, training the neural network and the final inference step.
elements.label: text

elements.char: We generated three training datasets, trading off the size of the dataset against the quality
elements.label: text

elements.char: of data (ie number of Monte Carlo scenarios per sample), while holding the total number of
elements.label: text

elements.char: Monte Carlo scenarios at 5x10
elements.label: text

elements.char: . Each dataset took approximately 1 week to generate using
elements.label: text

elements.char: all 24 cores of an AMD EPYC 7401P server.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Neural network model training is a function of the number of layers, the nodes per layer,
elements.label: text

elements.char: the size of the training set, the size of mini-batch and the learning rate. The models presented
elements.label: text

elements.char: in this paper were trained for between 3 hours and 1 week.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The time spent generating the training set and training the model are one-off costs. Once
elements.label: text

elements.char: completed they do not have to be repeated. These phases are most accurately compared to
elements.label: text

elements.char: the time spent developing traditional models.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Rarely do we discuss how long it took code
elements.label: text

elements.char: and test our basket MC model.
elements.label: text

elements.char: The time we are truly concerned with is the inference time: how quickly can a trained
elements.label: text

elements.char: model return a valuation. This varies with the size of the model. The small models we trained
elements.label: text

elements.char: (6 layers with 300 nodes per layer) were capable of returning more than 20,000 valuations in
elements.label: text

elements.char: parallel in less than 50 microseconds. The large models (6 layers with 1400 nodes per layer)
elements.label: text

elements.char: can compute 50,000 valuations in less than 6 milliseconds.

elements.char: Conclusions and Opportunities for Future Work
elements.label: text

elements.char: In this paper we have demonstrated that deep neural networks can be used to provide highly
elements.label: text

elements.char: accurate derivatives valuations using a basket option example. These models compute valu-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ations approximately 1 million times faster than traditional Monte Carlo models. We have
elements.label: text

elements.char: developed a successful methodology to generate a set of training data, which can be adapted
elements.label: text

elements.char: to suit other valuation models. Finally we have also demonstrated that using small numbers
elements.label: text

elements.char: of Monte Carlo paths in the training set is very effective and the the neural network learns
elements.label: text

elements.char: to average out the random error component of the Monte Carlo model found in the training
elements.label: text

elements.char: set.
elements.label: text

elements.char: We are actively investigating several areas:
elements.label: text

elements.char: 1. Scaling the dimensionality of the derivatives pricing model. Some models require many
elements.label: text

elements.char: hundreds of inputs across market data and trade specifics.
elements.label: text

elements.char: 2. Developing scoring techniques to determine the suitability of the trained model to input
elements.label: text

elements.char: data being appplied.
elements.label: text

elements.char: 3. Providing risk sensitivities through back propagation of neural networks as an alterna-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tive or complement to algorithmic differentiation.
elements.label: text

elements.char: 4. Using DNNs to approximate both valuation model and model calibration steps inde-
elements.label: text

elements.char: pendently as a pipeline.
elements.label: text

elements.char: 5. Applying transfer learning to accelerate the training of related derivative products.
elements.label: text

elements.char: 6. Using DNNs in practice to accelerate derivative valuations for XVA.
